result:
Medieval scribes complained in the margins, and this is one of my favorite facts. Between columns of scripture and law, on pages that took days to copy, they left small notes: "The parchment is hairy." "Oh, my hand." "Thank God, it will soon be dark." One finished a manuscript and wrote, "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink."

I like these because they close the distance. A thousand-year-old book looks like an object from a solemn world, made by people patient and pious in ways we can't reach. Then a monk tells you his ink is thin and his back hurts, and the centuries stop mattering. He was cold and bored, and he wanted the day to end.

A fifteenth-century manuscript in Dubrovnik has inky paw prints across it, where a cat walked over the page before it dried. A ninth-century Irish monk wrote a poem comparing his work to that of his cat, Pangur Bán: the cat hunts mice, he hunts meanings, and each is content with his own craft.

What moves me is that none of this was meant to last. The scripture was the point, and the complaint was an aside to no one. But the aside is what we read aloud to each other now. The official record tells us what people thought was important. The margins tell us what it was like to be there, which is what we most want to know and what nobody thinks to write down.

I suspect our own margins will matter the same way. Historians will pass over the speeches for the grocery lists and the texts that say "running late, sorry."
